title: Ivar Stenberg's Fast Start Rests on the Power Play
dek: The No. 2 pick has 8 points in 11 games, but the model sees a modest shooter whose team gets outchanced when he plays.
text:
Ivar Stenberg is 19 years old, born in Gothenburg, Sweden, a left-handed forward listed at 5'11" and 185 pounds. San Jose took him second overall in the 2026 draft, and he is now in the NHL, wearing No. 41. He has played 11 games, all this season and all for the Sharks, so his career line and his season line are the same: 3 goals, 5 assists, 8 points. Nothing in the data tells us about his path before the draft, so this piece sticks to what he has done since he arrived.

The headline number is the 8 points. Among forwards, that ranks 60th out of 392, which is a solid mark for a teenager in his first month. The more telling number is where those points came from. Six of the eight came on the power play. That leaves two points at even strength in 11 games. The production is real, but it is concentrated in one situation, and the power play is the part of a game a coach can hand a young player most easily.

**Chances versus results**

Expected goals is a measure of shot quality. Every shot gets a value based on where it was taken and what kind of shot it was, and the values add up to the number of goals an average shooter would have scored from those chances. Stenberg's own expected goals this season are 2.9. He has scored 3. His goals minus expected is 0.1, which is about as close to zero as it gets. He has not been lucky and he has not been snake-bitten. His goal total is what his chances say it should be.

That is worth stating because the points total alone can mislead. The goals are earned. But 2.9 expected goals in 11 games is not a high number for a player drafted this high. Among forwards, his own expected goals rank 108th of 392. His points rank is 60th. The gap between the two ranks tells you the points are running ahead of the shooting, and the assists and power play work are carrying that gap.

The model's own estimate of his shot-generating rate is 1 expected goal per 60 minutes. That is a modest rate for a scorer. The model also notes that it blends this season with last season and his role, because a few weeks of games is too few to trust alone. He has no NHL history to blend, so the early weeks carry more weight than they should and the estimate will move as games pile up.

**Role and ice time**

Stenberg averages 15.72 minutes a game. Among forwards that ranks 171st of 392, which is a middle-of-the-lineup workload rather than a featured one. Over his last 10 games the figure is 15.93, so his role has been steady. The log shows a range: his lowest night was 13.6 minutes against Florida in the opener, and his highest was 18.1 against Edmonton.

The power play points suggest he is on a unit, though the data does not say which one or in what spot, so I will not guess. What the minutes do say is that the Sharks are using him, but not leaning on him the way they would a first-line center or winger.

**Where the shots come from**

The shot map is the most interesting part of his profile. He has 24 unblocked shot attempts and an average shot distance of 27 feet. That average is dragged out by volume from a long way away: 13 of his attempts came from beyond 30 feet, and they were worth only 0.6 expected goals in total with no goals. Those are low-value looks.

The good looks are fewer. From inside 15 feet he has 8 shots, 2 goals and 1.4 expected goals. From 15 to 30 feet he has 3 shots, 1 goal and 0.9 expected goals. So the close range work is where his value lives. Two goals from 1.4 expected inside 15 feet is a small overperformance, and the one goal from 0.9 in the middle band is similar. The long-range shooting has produced nothing, which is normal for those distances.

Tracking data backs this up. His busiest shot areas on goal are the high slot with 5 shots and no goals, the left circle with 4 and no goals, and the low slot and crease with 2 shots each, one goal apiece. In other words, his goals have come from the dirty areas, and his most frequent shooting spots, the high slot and left circle, have not yet paid off. If he keeps getting to the slot, some of those should start to go in.

**How he skates and shoots**

Tracking has his top speed at 21.65 mph, which sits at the 49th percentile. That is league average, not a burner. He has 13 bursts over 20 mph, so he can get going, but nothing here suggests an elite skater. His hardest shot is 84.36 mph, at the 72nd percentile, which is solid and a little above the middle. Neither measure explains why he was picked second. Those qualities, whatever they are, are not showing up in speed or shot power.

**What the team does with him on the ice**

This is the part that complicates the 8 points. San Jose is 6-4-1 and takes 44.4% of the expected goals in its games, meaning the Sharks are generally outchanced. With Stenberg on the ice it is worse. At five-on-five his team has 34.3% of the expected goals, and the team's goals versus expected with him on the ice is minus 1.58, meaning the Sharks have scored about 1.6 fewer goals than the chances would predict when he plays. The team shares more of the expected goals without him than with him by 11.97 percentage points, so in these minutes the Sharks have been clearly worse.

Context matters. This is 11 games of a rookie whose team is already outchanced, and a gap of that size over such a small sample can shrink or flip quickly. It is still a warning that the production comes from the power play, not from driving play at even strength. The model's on-ice rate for chances for is 3.78 per 60, and he is on the ice for a point on 71% of goals scored while he plays, which shows how heavily his points track his team's scoring when he is out there.

**Recent form**

Over his last 10 games he has 8 points and 3 goals. The model expected 7.1 points and 2.6 goals from his chances and role, so he has beaten expectation slightly, by under a point. His expected goals in that stretch (2.9) is right at his usual level for that ice time (2.7). His team's chances for while he plays were 10.3 against a usual 10.0. Nothing in that stretch is out of line with a steady, ordinary level of play.

The game log shows how uneven it has been. He had a goal and an assist against Detroit and a goal against Ottawa, and went pointless in five of his 11 games. In the loss to Dallas he managed one shot and 0.12 expected goals.

**What to watch**

First, even-strength points. He has two. For his production to hold up beyond the power play, he needs to start creating at five-on-five, and the current numbers suggest that is where the Sharks struggle with him on the ice.

Second, the shot mix. Thirteen of his 24 attempts from beyond 30 feet is a lot of low-value shooting. If he trades some of that for slot and crease looks, his expected goals should rise and the 108th ranking should climb.

Third, the minutes. If the coaches give him more than 15.72 a night, it means they trust him. If they cut them back, the on-ice numbers are probably why.

What would change the picture: a few more weeks of games would give the model enough to work with, and a team share of expected goals that rises toward even with him on the ice would suggest the early gap was noise. On the other hand, if the power play cools off and the even-strength numbers stay where they are, the 8 points will look less impressive than they do today.
